```{r m2-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%")
library(postrank)
source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package = "postrank",
  mustWork = TRUE), local = TRUE)
one <- load_or_compute("tutorial_one")
two <- load_or_compute("tutorial_two")
commonality <- load_or_compute("tutorial_commonality")
sites <- pr_tutorial
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4L) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pct <- function(x, digits = 2L) paste0(fmt(100 * x, digits), "%")
ev <- two$evaluation
ct <- commonality$table
```

For one criterion, grading balances the expected cost of incorrect
directions against the cost of withholding comparisons. With several
criteria, the decision also depends on the target of the comparison.
Criterion-specific errors and errors in the ordering of a scalar composite
define different objectives, which may favor different reports even when
all target values are known.

We extend the loss in
[Posterior ranking, grades, and loss](m1-ranking-and-loss.html) to
criterion-weighted errors and compare it with loss for a scalar composite.
An exact calculation establishes the different posterior information
required by these objectives. The prepared six-site example illustrates
the cost of a common grading and comparison under a fixed loss. All
calculations use direct arithmetic, fixed-action evaluation or prepared
results; model fitting and optimization are not required.

## Criterion-weighted risk {#one-report-several-error-counts}

Let the targets be oriented so that larger values have higher priority.
A grade vector $g$ places unit $i$ above unit $j$ when $g_i<g_j$;
**grade 1 has highest priority**. Write $x_{ij}(g)=\mathbf{1}\{g_i<g_j\}$,
$M=\binom{n}{2}$ and $N(g)=\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}(g)$. Each disclosed
unordered pair enters this sum once, in its reported direction. Units in
the same grade have their comparison withheld.

For criterion $k$, define the error probability
$e_{ij,k}=\Pr(\theta_{ik}\le\theta_{jk}\mid Y)$ and the expected error count

$$
E_k(g)=\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}(g)e_{ij,k}.
$$

For one criterion, risk is $[E_1(g)+\tau\{M-N(g)\}]/M$. The convention here
counts a strict disclosed direction as wrong at latent equality. It also
charges for withholding without asserting equality. All examples below
have zero latent equality probability; [True ties and withheld comparisons](m4-ties-and-withholding.html)
explains how a different equality convention changes the loss.

For several criteria, choose nonnegative weights summing to one. The
criterion-weighted expected risk is

$$
R_{w,\tau}(g)
=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^K w_kE_k(g)+\tau\{M-N(g)\}}{M}
=\tau+\frac1M\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}(g)
\left(\sum_{k=1}^K w_ke_{ij,k}-\tau\right).
$$

The withheld-pair cost appears **once**, regardless of the number of criteria.
Weights normalize the directional-error scale; they do not multiply the
withholding charge by $K$. Setting $K=1$ and $w_1=1$ recovers the original
problem. An all-withheld action has risk $\tau$ whenever it is allowed.

This identity follows from linearity of expectation, with the observed
information, report, targets and preferences held fixed. Dependence among
criteria or pairs does not invalidate it. It does not imply that the errors
are independent, or that each disclosed direction is simultaneously correct
on every criterion. Lee (2026), Chapter 11,
[“Weighted directional risk from a supplied selection law”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#sec-weighted-directional-risk),
gives the loss and this finite-sum derivation.

Weights specify the relative cost of directional errors on the criteria;
scientific importance is not estimated from the posterior. Positive weight
on a criterion does not ensure that its expected error is as small as that
of another criterion. A bound on its error proportion requires an
additional constraint, as described in
[Computing grades and choosing settings](m5-computing-grades.html).

## Composite targets {#why-a-composite-is-a-different-target}

A scalar composite declares a target such as
$c_i=\sum_k a_k\theta_{ik}$. Its directional error probability is
$\Pr(c_i\le c_j\mid Y)$. This uses magnitudes and cardinal trade-offs;
$\sum_k w_ke_{ij,k}$ averages criterion-specific error probabilities.
Setting $a=w$ numerically does not make these quantities equal.

For a simple known state, take unit A with targets $(1,-2)$ and unit B with
$(0,0)$. With error weights $(3/4,1/4)$, reporting A above B costs $1/4$,
whereas the reverse costs $3/4$. Withholding at cost $0.3$ makes A above B
the least costly of the three actions. An equally weighted composite gives
A value $-1/2$ and B value zero, so its preferred direction is B above A.
All targets are known in this example; the difference arises from the
definition of a directional error under each objective. This is a member of the exact conflict family in Lee
(2026), Chapter 12,
[“Two co-primary targets for a reported direction”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/12-conflict-estimands.html#sec-two-estimands).

Agreement is possible. If, for every pair and almost every target state,
all positive-weight criteria have the same strict direction, a nonnegative
composite supported on those criteria with at least one positive coefficient
has that direction too. Under the same withholding cost and feasible family,
the two losses then agree. This sufficient condition is stronger than merely
having positively correlated estimates or mostly similar posterior means.

## Posterior information requirements {#which-posterior-information-is-needed}

Additive risk is determined by the within-criterion pair probabilities.
Once these are available, cross-criterion dependence is not required for
the expectation. Marginal distributions for individual units generally do
not determine these probabilities, however, because within-criterion
dependence between units affects their ordering.

Composite ordering and simultaneous correctness depend on additional
features of the joint law. To demonstrate this, consider two constructions
with identical within-criterion distributions but different dependence
between criteria. Unit B is fixed at $(0,0)$. Each matrix row specifies a
complete state for unit A with probability one half. These matrices define
finite laws rather than retained Monte Carlo draws.

```{r m2-two-laws}
together <- rbind(c(2, 2), c(-1, -1))
opposite <- rbind(c(2, -1), c(-1, 2))
w <- a <- c(.5, .5)
law_tau <- .2

law_summary <- function(A) {
  criterion_error <- colMeans(A <= 0)
  c(criterion_error,
    weighted_error = sum(w * criterion_error),
    composite_error = mean(as.vector(A %*% a) <= 0),
    correct_on_both = mean(rowSums(A > 0) == ncol(A)))
}
law_values <- rbind(together = law_summary(together),
  opposite = law_summary(opposite))
```

```{r m2-law-table, echo=FALSE}
law_table <- data.frame(
  Law = c("States move together", "States oppose"),
  `A's possible states` = c("(2,2) or (-1,-1)", "(2,-1) or (-1,2)"),
  `Error on criterion 1` = law_values[, 1L],
  `Error on criterion 2` = law_values[, 2L],
  `Composite error` = law_values[, "composite_error"],
  `Correct on both` = law_values[, "correct_on_both"], check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(law_table, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "The same proposed disclosure, A above B, evaluated under two exact laws. Every listed state has probability one half; B is zero on both criteria.")
```

The weighted error is `r fmt(law_values[1L, "weighted_error"], 1L)` under
both laws, as is the error for the reverse direction. Withholding therefore
minimizes additive risk at `tau =` `r fmt(law_tau, 1L)` in both. Under the
second law, however, A's composite is always positive: disclosing A above B
has composite error `r fmt(law_values[2L, "composite_error"], 0L)` and has lower expected loss than
withholding. The probability of being correct on both criteria also differs
between laws. Equal criterion-wise coefficients cannot recover either of
these joint calculations. The example is reproduced by direct arithmetic
from Lee (2026), Chapter 11,
[“Exact comparison of additive, composite, and joint-event information”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#an-exact-information-boundary-example).

For a composite calculated from posterior draws, retain genuine joint
states and apply the composite to each entire state. Pairing independent
criterion files by row number would impose a coupling that the files do not
establish. For a specified Gaussian joint law, means and the relevant
covariances can instead support an analytic calculation. That conclusion
uses the Gaussian law and its dependence assumptions, not means alone.

The function `postrank_composite()` constructs deterministic composite
scores from a matrix of posterior means. Although the typed Gaussian
input retains covariance information, this scoring function does not use
it and returns neither a posterior distribution nor composite-direction
probabilities. Precomputed pairwise inputs also lack the information
needed to reconstruct composite or joint-event probabilities. A posterior
analysis of the composite consequently requires a one-criterion posterior
specified for that target; see
[Posterior inputs and pairwise probabilities](m3-posterior-inputs.html).

## Scale changes affect the two goals differently

Applying the same strictly increasing function to every unit on a criterion
preserves its directions and equalities. If the posterior is transformed
accordingly and weights and feasible reports remain fixed, additive risks
and their full minimizing sets are unchanged. This ordinal property
of the target comparisons depends on the stated transformation conditions.

Rescaling composite components with the numerical coefficients held fixed
can alter their order. Similarly, refitting after transformation can change
the posterior law, and constructing a new score order from transformed
posterior means can change the feasible reports. None of these operations
satisfies the premises of the invariance result. The conditions are given
in Lee (2026), Chapter 12,
[“Ordinal invariance and qualified dominance statements”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/12-conflict-estimands.html#sec-invariance-dominance).

## Criterion-specific commonality costs {#read-the-burden-on-each-criterion}

The six fictional sites from [Getting started](a1-getting-started.html)
provide a small continuous example. Their normal distributions are specified directly,
with independent sites and independent criteria within sites. The common
report uses equal weights, withholding cost `r fmt(two$settings$tau, 1L)`
and at most `r two$settings$G_max` grades. Its expected errors per disclosed
pair are `r pct(ev$E_over_N[["score_A"]])` for score A and
`r pct(ev$E_over_N[["score_B"]])` for score B, over the same
`r ev$N` disclosed pairs. Equal weights have not equalized the errors.

Define each criterion's risk as
$R_k(g)=[E_k(g)+\tau\{M-N(g)\}]/M$. Then
$R_{w,\tau}(g)=\sum_k w_kR_k(g)$. For a fixed common report, its cost to
criterion $k$ relative to that criterion's own best feasible report is

$$
\Delta_k=R_k(g_{\mathrm{common}})-\min_{h\in\mathcal F}R_k(h).
$$

This difference is nonnegative when the common action belongs to the same
family $\mathcal F$. The package computes own-criterion comparisons at the
same withholding cost and grade-count settings. If the common problem has
criterion protections, `protection = "drop"` removes them by default;
`protection = "keep"` retains them. That choice changes the own comparison
family and should be reported. This tutorial has no such protections.

```{r m2-commonality-call, eval=FALSE}
commonality <- postrank_commonality_cost(two, backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 60, threads = 1, seed = 1304))
```

```{r m2-commonality, fig.cap="Extra criterion risk from using the prepared common grading for six fictional sites. Endpoints use each own-criterion solve's incumbent and lower bound; they are numerical solver bounds, not posterior intervals."}
postrank_plot_commonality(commonality)
```

The common action costs score A an additional
`r fmt(ct$cost_lower[ct$criterion_id == "score_A"])` risk units and score B
`r fmt(ct$cost_lower[ct$criterion_id == "score_B"])`, to the precision shown.
Each quantity includes withholding as well as errors; it is not a change
in score uncertainty or an estimate of social welfare.

If an own-criterion solve has incumbent risk $U_k$ and lower bound $L_k$,
the reported endpoints are $\max(0,R_k(g_{\mathrm{common}})-U_k)$ and
$R_k(g_{\mathrm{common}})-L_k$. Here they nearly coincide. A wide interval
would reflect incomplete optimization, and the interpretation inherits the
bounds' numerical limitations. With one criterion, the common and own
problems coincide under identical settings; there is no cross-criterion
compromise to measure.

## Score orders and evaluation loss {#separate-a-score-order-from-the-loss-it-is-evaluated-on}

A fixed-order baseline first chooses an order, then restricts its grades to
contiguous blocks of that order. `postrank_expected_rank()` obtains scores
from criterion-specific pair probabilities. `postrank_composite()` combines
posterior means using declared scales and centers. Either score order can
be followed by cuts chosen to minimize the **criterion-weighted** risk.
Using composite scores to select an order does not turn that risk into
composite-target risk.

The following optional calculation illustrates the distinction between
score construction and risk evaluation. The posterior means are those of
the specified tutorial law. The two weight vectors have different roles,
although their numerical values coincide. The cut calculation is omitted
when the article is built.

```{r m2-fixed-order, eval=FALSE}
a <- c(score_A = .5, score_B = .5)
scores <- postrank_composite(sites$law$means, weights = a,
  scales = c(score_A = 1, score_B = 1))
baseline <- postrank_cuts(scores, two$pairwise, settings = two$settings,
  direction = "descending", rule = "optimal")
```

Optimal cuts are optimal only within that declared order, respecting exact
score-tie blocks. Unrestricted grading also chooses the ordering of the
groups. Its exact optimum can be no worse under the same risk when its
family contains every baseline action. The interpretation of a numerical incumbent depends on its recorded
status and bound; an incomplete search does not establish exact optimality.
See Lee (2026), Chapter 16,
[“Conditional Bayes dominance and its limits”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/16-evaluation-frontiers.html#sec-conditional-bayes-dominance).

A report chosen for another objective can also be evaluated under
the reference objective. Here we take the prepared score-A-only grades as
a fixed action and use both criteria to evaluate them:

```{r m2-same-loss}
comparison <- postrank_compare(two,
  `Score A grades` = get_grades(one), baselines = character())
```

Their two-criterion risk is `r fmt(comparison$table$risk[2L])`, compared
with `r fmt(comparison$table$risk[1L])` for the common report, and both
actions satisfy the reference grade cap. Their disclosed counts are
`r comparison$table$N[2L]` and `r comparison$table$N[1L]`, respectively.
This calculation does not compare the original one-criterion scalar risk
with a two-criterion scalar risk, and `baselines = character()` avoids
constructing additional optimized cuts.

This comparison conditions on the units, targets, posterior law, weights,
withholding cost and feasible reports. It does not imply superiority under
another loss or evaluation law, for every realized target state, or for a
different institutional objective. Criterion-specific errors and disclosure
rates describe the consequences of the specified decision.
[Figures and sensitivity analysis](a7-figures-sensitivity.html) examines
their dependence on the settings.

## Source note

Lee, JoonHo (2026). *Decisions from Noisy Multidimensional Indicators:
Theory, Evidence, and Posterior Grading*, version 3, 29 October 2026.
Companion methods book. The specific Chapter 11, 12 and 16 sections
linked above supply the definitions, exact constructions, invariance
conditions and scope of the Bayes comparison. The commonality calculation
is also defined in `?postrank_commonality_cost`; its displayed numerical
results use the prepared tutorial law, not an empirical study.
